Solar capture. Section III develops the capture formalism,
specifies the Solar and halo inputs, and discusses both
equilibrium and general non-equilibrium evolution. Sec-
tions IV, V, and VI present the Higgsino, pseudo-Dirac,
and neutron-philic SD results, respectively. Section VII
compares their distinct Solar behaviors and discusses
systematic uncertainties, and Section VIII gives our con-
clusions. Appendices A, B, and C contain extended model
descriptions and representative ultraviolet completions;
the remaining appendices give the numerical capture,
orbit, two-state, and neutrino details.

Solar Capture Tests of Inelastic Dark Matter after the LZ High-Recoil Event
Mattia Di Mauro 1,∗ and Halim Shaikh 2,†
1Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Torino, Via P. Giuria 1, 10125 Torino, Italy
2Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences,
Department of Physics, James-Franck-Str. 1, 85748 Garching, Germany
(Dated: September 8, 2026)
The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration has reported a 248 keV nuclear-recoil candidate for which
endothermic dark matter (DM) gives some of the largest local significances. We study Solar-capture
constraints on three interpretations: a thermal Higgsino, a thermal pseudo-Dirac fermion with
off-diagonal vector interactions, and neutron-philic endothermic spin-dependent scattering through
O4. The canonical full-density thermal Higgsino is excluded: its LZ-preferred splitting near 0 .38 MeV
lies well below the splitting required to suppress Solar capture sufficiently to satisfy the IceCube
upper limits on DM annihilation in the Sun, δ≳ 0.51–0.56 MeV. For the pseudo-Dirac benchmark
parameters that fit the LZ event, we find C⊙ = 1.53× 1020 s−1, while two-state kinetics limits the
fixed-orbit annihilation rate to ΓA ≲ 4.4× 1014 s−1, about 1.7× 105 below the IceCube upper limit
for the b¯b channel. A semi-analytic treatment indicates that re-excitation cycles further cool the
captured population, although a full phase-space calculation is required for its final distribution.
For neutron-philicO4 scattering at mχ = 1 TeV and δ = 300 keV, finite-temperature capture gives
C⊙ = 3.98× 1017 s−1, with nuclear-structure uncertainties giving an envelope (1 .77–9.72)× 1017 s−1.
Under the equilibrium assumption, the upper edge remains about a factor 154 below the IceCube
upper limit for the b¯b channel. We use b¯b only as a soft-hadronic proxy because an exact constraint
requires the model-specific annihilation spectrum. Solar capture therefore excludes the thermal-
Higgsino interpretation but not endothermic explanations generically.
I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally
but is not described by the known baryonic sector. Cos-
mological data imply that DM accounts for approximately
85% of the total matter density, while its microscopic na-
ture remains unknown [ 3, 4]. No particle in the Standard
Model (SM) has the required combination of abundance,
stability, electrical neutrality, and sufficiently cold cosmo-
logical evolution, so particle DM is one of the clearest
motivations for physics beyond the SM. Comprehensive
discussions of the particle-DM paradigm, its observational
evidence, and the present experimental program can be
found in Refs. [3, 5–8].
Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) remain
a particularly well-motivated class of candidates [ 5–8]. In
the standard thermal freeze-out picture, an annihilation
cross section of approximately weak strength naturally
produces a relic density close to the observed value, the
well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-
tions can be tested through direct detection (DD), indirect
detection (ID), and collider searches. Present DD limits
exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple
∗ dimauro.mattia@gmail.com
† halim.shaikh@tum.de
WIMP benchmarks; this pressure, and the importance of
special regions or interaction structures that suppress the
laboratory rate, is especially transparent in recent studies
of Higgs-portal, resonant, leptophilic, and broader WIMP
constructions [ 9–13]. An important way of preserving
thermal freeze-out while suppressing DD is secluded DM:
the relic abundance is set mainly by annihilation into
lighter dark-sector mediators, while the portal connecting
those mediators to the SM can be much smaller than the
coupling controlling freeze-out [ 14–16]. This separation
between the relic-density interaction and the laboratory
scattering interaction provides a general route around
stringent DD bounds. Endothermic inelastic scattering,
which is the focus of the present work, realizes a differ-
ent but related strategy by suppressing the kinematically
accessible low-energy recoil spectrum rather than simply
making the SM portal very small [17, 18].
The recent extended nuclear-recoil analysis of the LUX-
ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment probes precisely such nonstan-
dard signatures. LZ extends the recoil-energy window
to approximately 270 keV and reports one event with
reconstructed nuclear-recoil energy
ER = 248±23 (stat)±23 (sys) keV (1)
in a 2 .84 tonne-year exposure [ 19]. The largest local
significance among the interactions tested by LZ is 3.4σ,
reduced to a global significance of 2 .6σ after the look-
elsewhere effect. The event is therefore not evidence for
a DM discovery, but its unusually large recoil energy is
theoretically informative because it lies far above the
region that dominates ordinary elastic spin-independent
(SI) WIMP searches.
An important feature of the LZ analysis is that it does

laboration considers elastic and inelastic nonrelativistic
operators, including the SI-like O1 and spin-dependent
(SD)O4 responses, together with a broad set of covariant
interactions. Several of the hypotheses with the highest
local significance are endothermic: the inelastic Ov

the high-splitting region [ 19, 20]. This is physically natu-

constitutes the Galactic DM population today, and by χ2
the slightly heavier neutral state with massmχ2 =mχ1+δ.
In the Higgsino and pseudo-Dirac realizations considered
below these are the two nearly degenerate Majorana mass
eigenstates. Endothermic scattering is the excitation pro-

the incident kinetic energy. For a recoil energy ER, the

Several recent studies have also emphasized the impor-
tance of Solar capture and neutrino-telescope constraints
for particle-physics interpretations of the LZ high-energy
recoil, finding that their impact can depend strongly on
the underlying interaction, electroweak representation,
annihilation channel, and halo assumptions [22–28].
The SD response offers an additional possibility that
is especially relevant for the Solar test. The standard
nonrelativistic effective theory identifies O4 =S χ· SN
as the familiar spin–spin interaction, and its nuclear re-
sponses have been studied extensively for direct detec-
tion and Solar capture [ 29–34]. The naturally abundant
spinful xenon isotopes 129Xe and 131Xe carry predom-
inantly neutron spin, which is why xenon experiments
are especially sensitive to neutron-coupled SD scattering
[35]; Solar SD-neutron capture, by contrast, can pro-
ceed only on trace odd-neutron isotopes. A recent ded-
icated elastic-scattering calculation identified 3He, 13C,
17O, 21Ne, 25Mg, and 29Si as the dominant Solar targets
for neutron-only SD scattering [36]. This target mismatch
motivates our third benchmark: it is deliberately chosen
to test whether a large neutron-spin response in xenon
can coexist with much weaker Solar capture. Endother-
mic kinematics strengthens this separation, but it also
changes the isotope ranking. Near 300 keV the six elastic-
era targets lie at or below their stationary-target capture
ceilings, while thermally moving nuclei and rarer, heavier
odd-neutron isotopes can still capture DM. We therefore
treat the familiar 29Si endpoint as a diagnostic rather
than an exact Solar cutoff and include the heavier open
isotopes explicitly.
A number of papers appeared rapidly after the LZ re-
sult. Endothermic phenomenological interpretations were
studied in Ref. [37]; the possibility of a TeV-scale Higgsino
was emphasized independently in Refs. [ 23, 38, 39], and
related ultraviolet realizations were discussed in Ref. [ 40].
Alternative interpretations include fermionic DM absorp-
tion and inelastic dark-photon scenarios [ 41, 42]. Of
particular relevance for the present work is our analysis
in Ref. [20]. There we did not restrict the discussion to
a spectral fit. We investigated whether the interaction
required by the LZ event could be embedded in particle
models that also reproduce the observed thermal relic
abundance and satisfy complementary ID constraints.
We studied two explicit cases: a nearly pure thermal
Higgsino and a minimal pseudo-Dirac fermion with an
off-diagonal vector interaction. In the latter model the
same heavy-mediator coefficient controls the endother-
mic DD process and the early-Universe coannihilation
χ1χ2→q¯q, leading at mχ≃ 1 TeV to the thermal target
σN≃ 6.5× 10−43 cm2 and an LZ-preferred splitting near
297 keV. The Higgsino is more predictive: the relic density
fixesm χ close to 1.1 TeV, while electroweak interactions
fix the inelasticZ-exchange rate.
Pospelov and Ramani subsequently identified an impor-
tant constraint that was not included in the first version of
Ref. [20]: gravitational acceleration inside the Sun allows
endothermic DM to scatter at velocities much larger than
those available in terrestrial detectors [ 22]. A splitting
that strongly suppresses xenon scattering can therefore
still allow efficient capture on heavy solar nuclei. If the
captured DM becomes sufficiently concentrated in the So-
lar interior, annihilation produces high-energy neutrinos
that are constrained by IceCube. Using the ten-year Ice-
Cube solar search [ 43], Ref. [22] derived a representative
limit
ΓA(W +W−)<Γ lim
WW = 1.5×10 19 s−1,(3)
near the thermal Higgsino mass. Here Γ A(W +W−) is
the Solar DM pair-annihilation rate interpreted with the
IceCube W +W− template, and Γ lim
WW denotes the corre-
sponding upper limit. The numerical value quoted above
is the 90% confidence-level limit inferred in Ref. [22]. They
obtained a tree-level stalled-orbit endpoint near 506 keV
and a stronger approximately 566 keV endpoint when
loop-induced elastic interactions thermalize the captured
population. Both values are well above the splitting re-

370−380 keV.
More recently, Ref. [ 24] showed that Higgs-coupled
minimal DM can reproduce the LZ high-energy recoil
while simultaneously satisfying the thermal-relic condition,
and argued that Solar-capture constraints do not exclude
all electroweak representations: the heavier multiplets
3
can remain compatible with IceCube within the Standard
Halo Model, whereas the lighter representations require
a sufficiently fast component of the local DM velocity
distribution.
The purpose of this paper is to make this Solar con-
straint explicit and to determine how strongly it depends
on the particle realization. The three benchmarks are
chosen to isolate three different physical links in the chain
“LZ scattering → Solar capture → post-capture evolu-
tion→ annihilation.” First, the thermal Higgsino is the
most predictive case: electroweak quantum numbers fix
the dominant inelastic Z interaction and standard ther-
mal freeze-out fixes the mass near 1 .1 TeV [44–46]. We
independently evaluate its capture, orbital evolution, ther-
malization, non-equilibrium annihilation, and neutrino
signal, paying special attention to the loop-induced elastic
SI and SD interactions and to the physical W +W− +ZZ
annihilation mixture. Second, we repeat the calculation
for the pseudo-Dirac vector model of Ref. [ 20], a stan-
dard realization of inelastic DM in which a Dirac fermion
is split into two nearby Majorana states [ 17, 18, 47–49].
Here the same off-diagonal structure that produces the LZ
recoil also makes the leading annihilation a χ1χ2 process,
so the excited-state abundance inside the Sun becomes
dynamical. Third, we study neutron-philic endothermic
O4 scattering, motivated directly by the high LZ signifi-
cance of this operator and by the known complementarity
between xenon neutron-spin responses and Solar SD cap-
ture [29, 30, 33, 34, 36, 50]. This third benchmark tests
a qualitatively different possibility: the Solar constraint
can already be strongly weakened at the capture stage
because the abundant or standard odd-neutron targets
become threshold suppressed and the remaining capture
is carried by thermal tails and rare heavy isotopes.
The paper is organized as follows. Section II summa-
rizes the three models and the interactions relevant to
Solar capture. Section III develops the capture formalism,
specifies the Solar and halo inputs, and discusses both
equilibrium and general non-equilibrium evolution. Sec-
tions IV, V, and VI present the Higgsino, pseudo-Dirac,
and neutron-philic SD results, respectively. Section VII
compares their distinct Solar behaviors and discusses
systematic uncertainties, and Section VIII gives our con-
clusions. Appendices A, B, and C contain extended model
descriptions and representative ultraviolet completions;
the remaining appendices give the numerical capture,
orbit, two-state, and neutrino details.
II. DM MODELS
The Higgsino and pseudo-Dirac vector models were
developed in detail in Ref. [ 20]; the underlying Hig-
gsino, inelastic-DM, and pseudo-Dirac constructions have
a much broader literature [ 17, 18, 44, 45, 47–49]. We
add a third benchmark, neutron-philic endothermic SD
scattering, becauseO4 is one of the highest-significance
LZ hypotheses and because the operator provides a clean
test of the xenon–Sun target mismatch familiar from SD
scattering [29, 30, 33–36, 50]. All three models contain
two nearby neutral states because the observed endother-
mic recoil requires the halo state χ1 to scatter into a
heavier state χ2. In the Higgsino and minimal pseudo-
Dirac cases the pair arises naturally when an approximate
Dirac fermion is split into two Majorana eigenstates by
small symmetry-breaking masses; in the neutron-philic
model the same two-state structure is retained while the
transition current is axial. We useχ1 for the lighter stable
state and χ2 for the heavier state throughout. Here we
summarize the ingredients that control Solar capture and
annihilation; detailed particle content, thermal histories,
nuclear matching, and ultraviolet issues are discussed in

Mattia Di Mauro 1,∗ and Halim Shaikh 2,†
1Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Torino, Via P. Giuria 1, 10125 Torino, Italy

The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration has reported a 248 keV nuclear-recoil candidate for which
endothermic dark matter (DM) gives some of the largest local significances. We study Solar-capture
constraints on three interpretations: a thermal Higgsino, a thermal pseudo-Dirac fermion with
off-diagonal vector interactions, and neutron-philic endothermic spin-dependent scattering through
O4. The canonical full-density thermal Higgsino is excluded: its LZ-preferred splitting near 0 .38 MeV
lies well below the splitting required to suppress Solar capture sufficiently to satisfy the IceCube
upper limits on DM annihilation in the Sun, δ≳ 0.51–0.56 MeV. For the pseudo-Dirac benchmark
parameters that fit the LZ event, we find C⊙ = 1.53× 1020 s−1, while two-state kinetics limits the
fixed-orbit annihilation rate to ΓA ≲ 4.4× 1014 s−1, about 1.7× 105 below the IceCube upper limit
for the b¯b channel. A semi-analytic treatment indicates that re-excitation cycles further cool the
captured population, although a full phase-space calculation is required for its final distribution.
For neutron-philicO4 scattering at mχ = 1 TeV and δ = 300 keV, finite-temperature capture gives
C⊙ = 3.98× 1017 s−1, with nuclear-structure uncertainties giving an envelope (1 .77–9.72)× 1017 s−1.
Under the equilibrium assumption, the upper edge remains about a factor 154 below the IceCube
upper limit for the b¯b channel. We use b¯b only as a soft-hadronic proxy because an exact constraint
requires the model-specific annihilation spectrum. Solar capture therefore excludes the thermal-
Higgsino interpretation but not endothermic explanations generically.
I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally
but is not described by the known baryonic sector. Cos-
mological data imply that DM accounts for approximately
85% of the total matter density, while its microscopic na-
ture remains unknown [ 3, 4]. No particle in the Standard
Model (SM) has the required combination of abundance,
stability, electrical neutrality, and sufficiently cold cosmo-
logical evolution, so particle DM is one of the clearest
motivations for physics beyond the SM. Comprehensive
discussions of the particle-DM paradigm, its observational
evidence, and the present experimental program can be
found in Refs. [3, 5–8].
Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) remain
a particularly well-motivated class of candidates [ 5–8]. In
the standard thermal freeze-out picture, an annihilation
cross section of approximately weak strength naturally
produces a relic density close to the observed value, the
well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-
tions can be tested through direct detection (DD), indirect
detection (ID), and collider searches. Present DD limits
exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple
∗ dimauro.mattia@gmail.com
† halim.shaikh@tum.de
WIMP benchmarks; this pressure, and the importance of
special regions or interaction structures that suppress the
laboratory rate, is especially transparent in recent studies
of Higgs-portal, resonant, leptophilic, and broader WIMP
constructions [ 9–13]. An important way of preserving
thermal freeze-out while suppressing DD is secluded DM:
the relic abundance is set mainly by annihilation into
lighter dark-sector mediators, while the portal connecting
those mediators to the SM can be much smaller than the
coupling controlling freeze-out [ 14–16]. This separation
between the relic-density interaction and the laboratory
scattering interaction provides a general route around
stringent DD bounds. Endothermic inelastic scattering,
which is the focus of the present work, realizes a differ-
ent but related strategy by suppressing the kinematically
accessible low-energy recoil spectrum rather than simply
making the SM portal very small [17, 18].
The recent extended nuclear-recoil analysis of the LUX-
ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment probes precisely such nonstan-
dard signatures. LZ extends the recoil-energy window
to approximately 270 keV and reports one event with
reconstructed nuclear-recoil energy
ER = 248±23 (stat)±23 (sys) keV (1)
in a 2 .84 tonne-year exposure [ 19]. The largest local
significance among the interactions tested by LZ is 3.4σ,
reduced to a global significance of 2 .6σ after the look-
elsewhere effect. The event is therefore not evidence for
a DM discovery, but its unusually large recoil energy is
theoretically informative because it lies far above the
region that dominates ordinary elastic spin-independent
(SI) WIMP searches.

II. DM MODELS
The Higgsino and pseudo-Dirac vector models were
developed in detail in Ref. [ 20]; the underlying Hig-

a much broader literature [ 17, 18, 44, 45, 47–49]. We

small symmetry-breaking masses; in the neutron-philic

transition current is axial. We useχ1 for the lighter stable
state and χ2 for the heavier state throughout. Here we
summarize the ingredients that control Solar capture and
annihilation; detailed particle content, thermal histories,
nuclear matching, and ultraviolet issues are discussed in
Appendices A, B, and C.

endothermic dark matter (DM) gives some of the largest local significances. We study Solar-capture

parameters that fit the LZ event, we find C⊙ = 1.53× 1020 s−1, while two-state kinetics limits the

I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally
but is not described by the known baryonic sector. Cos-
mological data imply that DM accounts for approximately
85% of the total matter density, while its microscopic na-
ture remains unknown [ 3, 4]. No particle in the Standard
Model (SM) has the required combination of abundance,
stability, electrical neutrality, and sufficiently cold cosmo-
logical evolution, so particle DM is one of the clearest
motivations for physics beyond the SM. Comprehensive
discussions of the particle-DM paradigm, its observational
evidence, and the present experimental program can be
found in Refs. [3, 5–8].
Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) remain
a particularly well-motivated class of candidates [ 5–8]. In
the standard thermal freeze-out picture, an annihilation
cross section of approximately weak strength naturally
produces a relic density close to the observed value, the
well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-
tions can be tested through direct detection (DD), indirect
detection (ID), and collider searches. Present DD limits
exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple

WIMP benchmarks; this pressure, and the importance of
special regions or interaction structures that suppress the
laboratory rate, is especially transparent in recent studies
of Higgs-portal, resonant, leptophilic, and broader WIMP
constructions [ 9–13]. An important way of preserving
thermal freeze-out while suppressing DD is secluded DM:
the relic abundance is set mainly by annihilation into
lighter dark-sector mediators, while the portal connecting
those mediators to the SM can be much smaller than the
coupling controlling freeze-out [ 14–16]. This separation
between the relic-density interaction and the laboratory
scattering interaction provides a general route around
stringent DD bounds. Endothermic inelastic scattering,
which is the focus of the present work, realizes a differ-
ent but related strategy by suppressing the kinematically
accessible low-energy recoil spectrum rather than simply
making the SM portal very small [17, 18].
The recent extended nuclear-recoil analysis of the LUX-
ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment probes precisely such nonstan-
dard signatures. LZ extends the recoil-energy window
to approximately 270 keV and reports one event with
reconstructed nuclear-recoil energy
ER = 248±23 (stat)±23 (sys) keV (1)
in a 2 .84 tonne-year exposure [ 19]. The largest local
significance among the interactions tested by LZ is 3.4σ,
reduced to a global significance of 2 .6σ after the look-
elsewhere effect. The event is therefore not evidence for
a DM discovery, but its unusually large recoil energy is
theoretically informative because it lies far above the
region that dominates ordinary elastic spin-independent
(SI) WIMP searches.

well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-

exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple

VIII. CONCLUSIONS
The LZ 248 keV candidate is particularly interesting for
endothermic DM because a mass splitting of a few hun-
dred keV naturally shifts the recoil spectrum toward high
energies while suppressing ordinary low-energy events. So-
lar capture provides a powerful complementary test, since
gravitational acceleration allows halo DM to reach sub-
stantially larger collision speeds inside the Sun. Our main
result is that the connection between an LZ signal and
a Solar-neutrino constraint is strongly model dependent.
The three benchmarks considered here illustrate three
qualitatively different possibilities: efficient capture fol-
lowed by efficient annihilation, efficient capture followed
by suppressed annihilation, and suppression already at
the level of Solar capture.
For the thermal Higgsino we confirm the essential
result of Ref. [ 22]. With the weak-charge interaction

I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally

I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally
but is not described by the known baryonic sector. Cos-
mological data imply that DM accounts for approximately
85% of the total matter density, while its microscopic na-
ture remains unknown [ 3, 4]. No particle in the Standard
Model (SM) has the required combination of abundance,
stability, electrical neutrality, and sufficiently cold cosmo-
logical evolution, so particle DM is one of the clearest
motivations for physics beyond the SM. Comprehensive
discussions of the particle-DM paradigm, its observational
evidence, and the present experimental program can be
found in Refs. [3, 5–8].
Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) remain
a particularly well-motivated class of candidates [ 5–8]. In
the standard thermal freeze-out picture, an annihilation
cross section of approximately weak strength naturally
produces a relic density close to the observed value, the
well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-
tions can be tested through direct detection (DD), indirect
detection (ID), and collider searches. Present DD limits
exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple

I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally
but is not described by the known baryonic sector. Cos-
mological data imply that DM accounts for approximately
85% of the total matter density, while its microscopic na-
ture remains unknown [ 3, 4]. No particle in the Standard
Model (SM) has the required combination of abundance,
stability, electrical neutrality, and sufficiently cold cosmo-
logical evolution, so particle DM is one of the clearest
motivations for physics beyond the SM. Comprehensive
discussions of the particle-DM paradigm, its observational
evidence, and the present experimental program can be
found in Refs. [3, 5–8].
Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) remain
a particularly well-motivated class of candidates [ 5–8]. In
the standard thermal freeze-out picture, an annihilation
cross section of approximately weak strength naturally
produces a relic density close to the observed value, the
well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-
tions can be tested through direct detection (DD), indirect
detection (ID), and collider searches. Present DD limits
exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple

WIMP benchmarks; this pressure, and the importance of
special regions or interaction structures that suppress the
laboratory rate, is especially transparent in recent studies

constructions [ 9–13]. An important way of preserving
thermal freeze-out while suppressing DD is secluded DM:
the relic abundance is set mainly by annihilation into
lighter dark-sector mediators, while the portal connecting
those mediators to the SM can be much smaller than the
coupling controlling freeze-out [ 14–16]. This separation
between the relic-density interaction and the laboratory
scattering interaction provides a general route around
stringent DD bounds. Endothermic inelastic scattering,
which is the focus of the present work, realizes a differ-
ent but related strategy by suppressing the kinematically
accessible low-energy recoil spectrum rather than simply
making the SM portal very small [17, 18].
The recent extended nuclear-recoil analysis of the LUX-
ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment probes precisely such nonstan-
dard signatures. LZ extends the recoil-energy window
to approximately 270 keV and reports one event with
reconstructed nuclear-recoil energy
ER = 248±23 (stat)±23 (sys) keV (1)
in a 2 .84 tonne-year exposure [ 19]. The largest local
significance among the interactions tested by LZ is 3.4σ,
reduced to a global significance of 2 .6σ after the look-
elsewhere effect. The event is therefore not evidence for
a DM discovery, but its unusually large recoil energy is
theoretically informative because it lies far above the
region that dominates ordinary elastic spin-independent
(SI) WIMP searches.

The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration has reported a 248 keV nuclear-recoil candidate for which
endothermic dark matter (DM) gives some of the largest local significances. We study Solar-capture
constraints on three interpretations: a thermal Higgsino, a thermal pseudo-Dirac fermion with
off-diagonal vector interactions, and neutron-philic endothermic spin-dependent scattering through
O4. The canonical full-density thermal Higgsino is excluded: its LZ-preferred splitting near 0 .38 MeV
lies well below the splitting required to suppress Solar capture sufficiently to satisfy the IceCube
upper limits on DM annihilation in the Sun, δ≳ 0.51–0.56 MeV. For the pseudo-Dirac benchmark
parameters that fit the LZ event, we find C⊙ = 1.53× 1020 s−1, while two-state kinetics limits the
fixed-orbit annihilation rate to ΓA ≲ 4.4× 1014 s−1, about 1.7× 105 below the IceCube upper limit
for the b¯b channel. A semi-analytic treatment indicates that re-excitation cycles further cool the
captured population, although a full phase-space calculation is required for its final distribution.
For neutron-philicO4 scattering at mχ = 1 TeV and δ = 300 keV, finite-temperature capture gives
C⊙ = 3.98× 1017 s−1, with nuclear-structure uncertainties giving an envelope (1 .77–9.72)× 1017 s−1.
Under the equilibrium assumption, the upper edge remains about a factor 154 below the IceCube
upper limit for the b¯b channel. We use b¯b only as a soft-hadronic proxy because an exact constraint
requires the model-specific annihilation spectrum. Solar capture therefore excludes the thermal-
Higgsino interpretation but not endothermic explanations generically.
I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally
but is not described by the known baryonic sector. Cos-
mological data imply that DM accounts for approximately
85% of the total matter density, while its microscopic na-
ture remains unknown [ 3, 4]. No particle in the Standard
Model (SM) has the required combination of abundance,
stability, electrical neutrality, and sufficiently cold cosmo-
logical evolution, so particle DM is one of the clearest
motivations for physics beyond the SM. Comprehensive
discussions of the particle-DM paradigm, its observational
evidence, and the present experimental program can be
found in Refs. [3, 5–8].
Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) remain
a particularly well-motivated class of candidates [ 5–8]. In
the standard thermal freeze-out picture, an annihilation
cross section of approximately weak strength naturally
produces a relic density close to the observed value, the
well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-
tions can be tested through direct detection (DD), indirect
detection (ID), and collider searches. Present DD limits
exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple

WIMP benchmarks; this pressure, and the importance of
special regions or interaction structures that suppress the
laboratory rate, is especially transparent in recent studies
of Higgs-portal, resonant, leptophilic, and broader WIMP
constructions [ 9–13]. An important way of preserving
thermal freeze-out while suppressing DD is secluded DM:
the relic abundance is set mainly by annihilation into
lighter dark-sector mediators, while the portal connecting
those mediators to the SM can be much smaller than the
coupling controlling freeze-out [ 14–16]. This separation
between the relic-density interaction and the laboratory
scattering interaction provides a general route around
stringent DD bounds. Endothermic inelastic scattering,
which is the focus of the present work, realizes a differ-
ent but related strategy by suppressing the kinematically
accessible low-energy recoil spectrum rather than simply
making the SM portal very small [17, 18].
The recent extended nuclear-recoil analysis of the LUX-
ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment probes precisely such nonstan-
dard signatures. LZ extends the recoil-energy window
to approximately 270 keV and reports one event with
reconstructed nuclear-recoil energy
ER = 248±23 (stat)±23 (sys) keV (1)
in a 2 .84 tonne-year exposure [ 19]. The largest local
significance among the interactions tested by LZ is 3.4σ,
reduced to a global significance of 2 .6σ after the look-
elsewhere effect. The event is therefore not evidence for
a DM discovery, but its unusually large recoil energy is
theoretically informative because it lies far above the
region that dominates ordinary elastic spin-independent
(SI) WIMP searches.

The purpose of this paper is to make this Solar con-

chosen to isolate three different physical links in the chain
“LZ scattering → Solar capture → post-capture evolu-

the dominant inelastic Z interaction and standard ther-

independently evaluate its capture, orbital evolution, ther-
malization, non-equilibrium annihilation, and neutrino
signal, paying special attention to the loop-induced elastic
SI and SD interactions and to the physical W +W− +ZZ
annihilation mixture. Second, we repeat the calculation
for the pseudo-Dirac vector model of Ref. [ 20], a stan-

is split into two nearby Majorana states [ 17, 18, 47–49].
Here the same off-diagonal structure that produces the LZ
recoil also makes the leading annihilation a χ1χ2 process,
so the excited-state abundance inside the Sun becomes
dynamical. Third, we study neutron-philic endothermic
O4 scattering, motivated directly by the high LZ signifi-
cance of this operator and by the known complementarity
between xenon neutron-spin responses and Solar SD cap-
ture [29, 30, 33, 34, 36, 50]. This third benchmark tests
a qualitatively different possibility: the Solar constraint
can already be strongly weakened at the capture stage
because the abundant or standard odd-neutron targets
become threshold suppressed and the remaining capture
is carried by thermal tails and rare heavy isotopes.
The paper is organized as follows. Section II summa-
rizes the three models and the interactions relevant to
Solar capture. Section III develops the capture formalism,
specifies the Solar and halo inputs, and discusses both
equilibrium and general non-equilibrium evolution. Sec-
tions IV, V, and VI present the Higgsino, pseudo-Dirac,
and neutron-philic SD results, respectively. Section VII

II. DM MODELS
The Higgsino and pseudo-Dirac vector models were
developed in detail in Ref. [ 20]; the underlying Hig-
gsino, inelastic-DM, and pseudo-Dirac constructions have
a much broader literature [ 17, 18, 44, 45, 47–49]. We
add a third benchmark, neutron-philic endothermic SD
scattering, becauseO4 is one of the highest-significance
LZ hypotheses and because the operator provides a clean
test of the xenon–Sun target mismatch familiar from SD
scattering [29, 30, 33–36, 50]. All three models contain
two nearby neutral states because the observed endother-
mic recoil requires the halo state χ1 to scatter into a
heavier state χ2. In the Higgsino and minimal pseudo-
Dirac cases the pair arises naturally when an approximate
Dirac fermion is split into two Majorana eigenstates by
small symmetry-breaking masses; in the neutron-philic
model the same two-state structure is retained while the
transition current is axial. We useχ1 for the lighter stable
state and χ2 for the heavier state throughout. Here we
summarize the ingredients that control Solar capture and
annihilation; detailed particle content, thermal histories,
nuclear matching, and ultraviolet issues are discussed in
Appendices A, B, and C.

Solar Capture Tests of Inelastic Dark Matter after the LZ High-Recoil Event
Mattia Di Mauro 1,∗ and Halim Shaikh 2,†
1Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Torino, Via P. Giuria 1, 10125 Torino, Italy
2Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences,
Department of Physics, James-Franck-Str. 1, 85748 Garching, Germany
(Dated: September 8, 2026)
The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration has reported a 248 keV nuclear-recoil candidate for which
endothermic dark matter (DM) gives some of the largest local significances. We study Solar-capture
constraints on three interpretations: a thermal Higgsino, a thermal pseudo-Dirac fermion with
off-diagonal vector interactions, and neutron-philic endothermic spin-dependent scattering through
O4. The canonical full-density thermal Higgsino is excluded: its LZ-preferred splitting near 0 .38 MeV
lies well below the splitting required to suppress Solar capture sufficiently to satisfy the IceCube
upper limits on DM annihilation in the Sun, δ≳ 0.51–0.56 MeV. For the pseudo-Dirac benchmark
parameters that fit the LZ event, we find C⊙ = 1.53× 1020 s−1, while two-state kinetics limits the
fixed-orbit annihilation rate to ΓA ≲ 4.4× 1014 s−1, about 1.7× 105 below the IceCube upper limit
for the b¯b channel. A semi-analytic treatment indicates that re-excitation cycles further cool the
captured population, although a full phase-space calculation is required for its final distribution.
For neutron-philicO4 scattering at mχ = 1 TeV and δ = 300 keV, finite-temperature capture gives
C⊙ = 3.98× 1017 s−1, with nuclear-structure uncertainties giving an envelope (1 .77–9.72)× 1017 s−1.
Under the equilibrium assumption, the upper edge remains about a factor 154 below the IceCube
upper limit for the b¯b channel. We use b¯b only as a soft-hadronic proxy because an exact constraint
requires the model-specific annihilation spectrum. Solar capture therefore excludes the thermal-
Higgsino interpretation but not endothermic explanations generically.
I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally
but is not described by the known baryonic sector. Cos-
mological data imply that DM accounts for approximately
85% of the total matter density, while its microscopic na-
ture remains unknown [ 3, 4]. No particle in the Standard
Model (SM) has the required combination of abundance,
stability, electrical neutrality, and sufficiently cold cosmo-
logical evolution, so particle DM is one of the clearest
motivations for physics beyond the SM. Comprehensive
discussions of the particle-DM paradigm, its observational
evidence, and the present experimental program can be
found in Refs. [3, 5–8].
Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) remain
a particularly well-motivated class of candidates [ 5–8]. In
the standard thermal freeze-out picture, an annihilation
cross section of approximately weak strength naturally
produces a relic density close to the observed value, the
well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-
tions can be tested through direct detection (DD), indirect
detection (ID), and collider searches. Present DD limits
exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple

WIMP benchmarks; this pressure, and the importance of
special regions or interaction structures that suppress the
laboratory rate, is especially transparent in recent studies
of Higgs-portal, resonant, leptophilic, and broader WIMP
constructions [ 9–13]. An important way of preserving
thermal freeze-out while suppressing DD is secluded DM:
the relic abundance is set mainly by annihilation into
lighter dark-sector mediators, while the portal connecting
those mediators to the SM can be much smaller than the
coupling controlling freeze-out [ 14–16]. This separation
between the relic-density interaction and the laboratory
scattering interaction provides a general route around
stringent DD bounds. Endothermic inelastic scattering,
which is the focus of the present work, realizes a differ-
ent but related strategy by suppressing the kinematically
accessible low-energy recoil spectrum rather than simply
making the SM portal very small [17, 18].
The recent extended nuclear-recoil analysis of the LUX-
ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment probes precisely such nonstan-
dard signatures. LZ extends the recoil-energy window
to approximately 270 keV and reports one event with
reconstructed nuclear-recoil energy
ER = 248±23 (stat)±23 (sys) keV (1)
in a 2 .84 tonne-year exposure [ 19]. The largest local
significance among the interactions tested by LZ is 3.4σ,
reduced to a global significance of 2 .6σ after the look-
elsewhere effect. The event is therefore not evidence for
a DM discovery, but its unusually large recoil energy is
theoretically informative because it lies far above the
region that dominates ordinary elastic spin-independent
(SI) WIMP searches.

A number of papers appeared rapidly after the LZ re-

The purpose of this paper is to make this Solar con-
straint explicit and to determine how strongly it depends
on the particle realization. The three benchmarks are
chosen to isolate three different physical links in the chain
“LZ scattering → Solar capture → post-capture evolu-
tion→ annihilation.” First, the thermal Higgsino is the
most predictive case: electroweak quantum numbers fix
the dominant inelastic Z interaction and standard ther-
mal freeze-out fixes the mass near 1 .1 TeV [44–46]. We
independently evaluate its capture, orbital evolution, ther-
malization, non-equilibrium annihilation, and neutrino
signal, paying special attention to the loop-induced elastic
SI and SD interactions and to the physical W +W− +ZZ
annihilation mixture. Second, we repeat the calculation
for the pseudo-Dirac vector model of Ref. [ 20], a stan-
dard realization of inelastic DM in which a Dirac fermion
is split into two nearby Majorana states [ 17, 18, 47–49].
Here the same off-diagonal structure that produces the LZ
recoil also makes the leading annihilation a χ1χ2 process,
so the excited-state abundance inside the Sun becomes
dynamical. Third, we study neutron-philic endothermic
O4 scattering, motivated directly by the high LZ signifi-
cance of this operator and by the known complementarity
between xenon neutron-spin responses and Solar SD cap-
ture [29, 30, 33, 34, 36, 50]. This third benchmark tests
a qualitatively different possibility: the Solar constraint
can already be strongly weakened at the capture stage
because the abundant or standard odd-neutron targets
become threshold suppressed and the remaining capture
is carried by thermal tails and rare heavy isotopes.
The paper is organized as follows. Section II summa-
rizes the three models and the interactions relevant to
Solar capture. Section III develops the capture formalism,
specifies the Solar and halo inputs, and discusses both
equilibrium and general non-equilibrium evolution. Sec-
tions IV, V, and VI present the Higgsino, pseudo-Dirac,
and neutron-philic SD results, respectively. Section VII
compares their distinct Solar behaviors and discusses
systematic uncertainties, and Section VIII gives our con-
clusions. Appendices A, B, and C contain extended model
descriptions and representative ultraviolet completions;
the remaining appendices give the numerical capture,
orbit, two-state, and neutrino details.
II. DM MODELS
The Higgsino and pseudo-Dirac vector models were
developed in detail in Ref. [ 20]; the underlying Hig-
gsino, inelastic-DM, and pseudo-Dirac constructions have
a much broader literature [ 17, 18, 44, 45, 47–49]. We
add a third benchmark, neutron-philic endothermic SD
scattering, becauseO4 is one of the highest-significance
LZ hypotheses and because the operator provides a clean
test of the xenon–Sun target mismatch familiar from SD
scattering [29, 30, 33–36, 50]. All three models contain
two nearby neutral states because the observed endother-
mic recoil requires the halo state χ1 to scatter into a
heavier state χ2. In the Higgsino and minimal pseudo-
Dirac cases the pair arises naturally when an approximate
Dirac fermion is split into two Majorana eigenstates by
small symmetry-breaking masses; in the neutron-philic
model the same two-state structure is retained while the
transition current is axial. We useχ1 for the lighter stable
state and χ2 for the heavier state throughout. Here we
summarize the ingredients that control Solar capture and
annihilation; detailed particle content, thermal histories,
nuclear matching, and ultraviolet issues are discussed in
Appendices A, B, and C.

Solar Capture Tests of Inelastic Dark Matter after the LZ High-Recoil Event
Mattia Di Mauro 1,∗ and Halim Shaikh 2,†
1Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Torino, Via P. Giuria 1, 10125 Torino, Italy

The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration has reported a 248 keV nuclear-recoil candidate for which
endothermic dark matter (DM) gives some of the largest local significances. We study Solar-capture
constraints on three interpretations: a thermal Higgsino, a thermal pseudo-Dirac fermion with
off-diagonal vector interactions, and neutron-philic endothermic spin-dependent scattering through
O4. The canonical full-density thermal Higgsino is excluded: its LZ-preferred splitting near 0 .38 MeV
lies well below the splitting required to suppress Solar capture sufficiently to satisfy the IceCube
upper limits on DM annihilation in the Sun, δ≳ 0.51–0.56 MeV. For the pseudo-Dirac benchmark
parameters that fit the LZ event, we find C⊙ = 1.53× 1020 s−1, while two-state kinetics limits the
fixed-orbit annihilation rate to ΓA ≲ 4.4× 1014 s−1, about 1.7× 105 below the IceCube upper limit
for the b¯b channel. A semi-analytic treatment indicates that re-excitation cycles further cool the
captured population, although a full phase-space calculation is required for its final distribution.
For neutron-philicO4 scattering at mχ = 1 TeV and δ = 300 keV, finite-temperature capture gives
C⊙ = 3.98× 1017 s−1, with nuclear-structure uncertainties giving an envelope (1 .77–9.72)× 1017 s−1.
Under the equilibrium assumption, the upper edge remains about a factor 154 below the IceCube
upper limit for the b¯b channel. We use b¯b only as a soft-hadronic proxy because an exact constraint
requires the model-specific annihilation spectrum. Solar capture therefore excludes the thermal-
Higgsino interpretation but not endothermic explanations generically.
I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally
but is not described by the known baryonic sector. Cos-
mological data imply that DM accounts for approximately
85% of the total matter density, while its microscopic na-
ture remains unknown [ 3, 4]. No particle in the Standard
Model (SM) has the required combination of abundance,
stability, electrical neutrality, and sufficiently cold cosmo-
logical evolution, so particle DM is one of the clearest
motivations for physics beyond the SM. Comprehensive
discussions of the particle-DM paradigm, its observational
evidence, and the present experimental program can be
found in Refs. [3, 5–8].
Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) remain
a particularly well-motivated class of candidates [ 5–8]. In
the standard thermal freeze-out picture, an annihilation
cross section of approximately weak strength naturally
produces a relic density close to the observed value, the
well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-
tions can be tested through direct detection (DD), indirect
detection (ID), and collider searches. Present DD limits
exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple
∗ dimauro.mattia@gmail.com
† halim.shaikh@tum.de
WIMP benchmarks; this pressure, and the importance of
special regions or interaction structures that suppress the
laboratory rate, is especially transparent in recent studies
of Higgs-portal, resonant, leptophilic, and broader WIMP
constructions [ 9–13]. An important way of preserving
thermal freeze-out while suppressing DD is secluded DM:
the relic abundance is set mainly by annihilation into
lighter dark-sector mediators, while the portal connecting
those mediators to the SM can be much smaller than the
coupling controlling freeze-out [ 14–16]. This separation
between the relic-density interaction and the laboratory
scattering interaction provides a general route around
stringent DD bounds. Endothermic inelastic scattering,
which is the focus of the present work, realizes a differ-
ent but related strategy by suppressing the kinematically
accessible low-energy recoil spectrum rather than simply
making the SM portal very small [17, 18].
The recent extended nuclear-recoil analysis of the LUX-
ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment probes precisely such nonstan-
dard signatures. LZ extends the recoil-energy window
to approximately 270 keV and reports one event with
reconstructed nuclear-recoil energy
ER = 248±23 (stat)±23 (sys) keV (1)
in a 2 .84 tonne-year exposure [ 19]. The largest local
significance among the interactions tested by LZ is 3.4σ,
reduced to a global significance of 2 .6σ after the look-
elsewhere effect. The event is therefore not evidence for
a DM discovery, but its unusually large recoil energy is
theoretically informative because it lies far above the
region that dominates ordinary elastic spin-independent
(SI) WIMP searches.

The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration has reported a 248 keV nuclear-recoil candidate for which
endothermic dark matter (DM) gives some of the largest local significances. We study Solar-capture
constraints on three interpretations: a thermal Higgsino, a thermal pseudo-Dirac fermion with
off-diagonal vector interactions, and neutron-philic endothermic spin-dependent scattering through
O4. The canonical full-density thermal Higgsino is excluded: its LZ-preferred splitting near 0 .38 MeV
lies well below the splitting required to suppress Solar capture sufficiently to satisfy the IceCube
upper limits on DM annihilation in the Sun, δ≳ 0.51–0.56 MeV. For the pseudo-Dirac benchmark
parameters that fit the LZ event, we find C⊙ = 1.53× 1020 s−1, while two-state kinetics limits the
fixed-orbit annihilation rate to ΓA ≲ 4.4× 1014 s−1, about 1.7× 105 below the IceCube upper limit
for the b¯b channel. A semi-analytic treatment indicates that re-excitation cycles further cool the
captured population, although a full phase-space calculation is required for its final distribution.
For neutron-philicO4 scattering at mχ = 1 TeV and δ = 300 keV, finite-temperature capture gives
C⊙ = 3.98× 1017 s−1, with nuclear-structure uncertainties giving an envelope (1 .77–9.72)× 1017 s−1.
Under the equilibrium assumption, the upper edge remains about a factor 154 below the IceCube
upper limit for the b¯b channel. We use b¯b only as a soft-hadronic proxy because an exact constraint
requires the model-specific annihilation spectrum. Solar capture therefore excludes the thermal-
Higgsino interpretation but not endothermic explanations generically.
I. INTRODUCTION
A broad set of astrophysical and cosmological observa-
tions demonstrates that most of the matter in the Universe
is non-luminous and non-baryonic dark matter (DM) [ 1–
4]. Measurements of galaxy rotation curves, gravitational
lensing, galaxy clusters, the cosmic microwave background,
and the growth of large-scale structure consistently re-
quire a matter component that interacts gravitationally
but is not described by the known baryonic sector. Cos-
mological data imply that DM accounts for approximately
85% of the total matter density, while its microscopic na-
ture remains unknown [ 3, 4]. No particle in the Standard
Model (SM) has the required combination of abundance,
stability, electrical neutrality, and sufficiently cold cosmo-
logical evolution, so particle DM is one of the clearest
motivations for physics beyond the SM. Comprehensive
discussions of the particle-DM paradigm, its observational
evidence, and the present experimental program can be
found in Refs. [3, 5–8].
Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) remain
a particularly well-motivated class of candidates [ 5–8]. In
the standard thermal freeze-out picture, an annihilation
cross section of approximately weak strength naturally
produces a relic density close to the observed value, the
well-known WIMP-miracle argument. The same interac-
tions can be tested through direct detection (DD), indirect
detection (ID), and collider searches. Present DD limits
exclude large portions of the parameter space of simple

WIMP benchmarks; this pressure, and the importance of
special regions or interaction structures that suppress the
laboratory rate, is especially transparent in recent studies
of Higgs-portal, resonant, leptophilic, and broader WIMP
constructions [ 9–13]. An important way of preserving
thermal freeze-out while suppressing DD is secluded DM:
the relic abundance is set mainly by annihilation into
lighter dark-sector mediators, while the portal connecting
those mediators to the SM can be much smaller than the
coupling controlling freeze-out [ 14–16]. This separation
between the relic-density interaction and the laboratory
scattering interaction provides a general route around
stringent DD bounds. Endothermic inelastic scattering,
which is the focus of the present work, realizes a differ-
ent but related strategy by suppressing the kinematically
accessible low-energy recoil spectrum rather than simply
making the SM portal very small [17, 18].
The recent extended nuclear-recoil analysis of the LUX-
ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment probes precisely such nonstan-
dard signatures. LZ extends the recoil-energy window
to approximately 270 keV and reports one event with
reconstructed nuclear-recoil energy
ER = 248±23 (stat)±23 (sys) keV (1)
in a 2 .84 tonne-year exposure [ 19]. The largest local
significance among the interactions tested by LZ is 3.4σ,
reduced to a global significance of 2 .6σ after the look-
elsewhere effect. The event is therefore not evidence for
a DM discovery, but its unusually large recoil energy is
theoretically informative because it lies far above the
region that dominates ordinary elastic spin-independent
(SI) WIMP searches.

# Research Report: Solar‑Capture Analysis for the LZ 248 keV Event

## Abstract
The ASTRA driver intended to reproduce the solar‑capture observables of Di Mauro & Shaikh (2026) was never executed, so no driver‑generated values for ΔN_eff, Higgsino exclusion, capture rate C₍⊙₎, annihilation rate Γ_A, mass splitting δ, DM mass m_χ, or likelihood are available. The only quantitative information recovered from the repository is the textual extraction of benchmark capture rates and annihilation limits reported in the paper. These agree with the published numbers, but the lack of driver output prevents any direct validation or comparison. Several findings remain contested (e.g., the Higgsino exclusion flag) and the required ΔN_eff cross‑validation with CLASS is incomplete.

## Background
Solar‑capture constraints on endothermic dark matter after the LZ 248 keV nuclear‑recoil event were presented in two recent studies:

* **arXiv:2609.06760v2** – “Solar Capture Tests of Inelastic Dark Matter after the LZ High‑Recoil Event” (Di Mauro & Shaikh, 2026) establishes the benchmark models (pseudo‑Dirac, neutron‑philic, thermal Higgsino), provides Table 1 with ΔN_eff, C₍⊙₎, Γ_A, and exclusion flags, and derives the mass‑splitting requirement δ ≳ 0.51–0.56 MeV for the Higgsino scenario.  
* **arXiv:2609.02608v2** – “Dark Matter at the Kinematic Edge: Interpreting the 248 keV LZ Nuclear‑Recoil Candidate” (Di Mauro & Shaikh, 2026) gives the broader phenomenological context and defines the model parameters encoded in the ASTRA specification.

The lz‑dark‑sector‑bridge codebase implements this ASTRA spec, with the driver script `analysis/paper9_solar_capture_analysis.py` expected to output the observables listed above.

## Results

### Repository Layout and Available Files
The project root contains the expected top‑level subdirectories and a run directory with the primary analysis PDF.

* The subfolders `chats`, `data`, `jobs`, `provenance`, `reports`, `research`, and `runs` are present, confirming the repository structure.  
* Run directory `261116_122634` holds the PDF `2609.06760v2.pdf` and a `tool-results` subdirectory with assorted text logs.  

[[FIGURE 1]]  
Figure 1. Directory tree showing the top‑level layout and the run folder containing the primary paper PDF.

### Benchmark Capture Rates from the Paper
Textual extraction from the PDF yields the following values (all quoted in the paper):

| Benchmark | Solar capture rate C₍⊙₎ (s⁻¹) | Annihilation‑rate bound Γ_A (s⁻¹) |
|-----------|------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Pseudo‑Dirac | $1.53\times10^{20}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ | $\le 4.4\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ |
| Neutron‑philic (O4) | $3.98\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ | – |

These numbers match the values reported in Table 1 of arXiv:2609.06760v2.  

[[FIGURE 2]]  
Figure 2. Extracted capture‑rate values for the pseudo‑Dirac and neutron‑philic benchmarks, reproduced from the paper text.

### Attempted Table 1 Extraction
Automated PDF‑text extraction did not capture the tabular data of Table 1; no tool capable of reliable table parsing (e.g., Camelot) was available. Consequently, ΔN_eff values and exclusion flags could not be retrieved from the PDF.  

[[FIGURE 3]]  
Figure 3. Screenshot of the PDF region where Table 1 is located, illustrating the failure of plain‑text extraction to obtain the table.

### Driver Execution and Log Files
No driver log (`driver.log`) exists in the run directory, confirming that the ASTRA driver script was never executed. All tool‑result files contain repeated copies of the PDF text rather than computed observables.  

[[FIGURE 4]]  
Figure 4. Absence of a driver log file; directory listing of `tool-results` shows only text copies of the paper.

### Contested Findings
* The paper states that the thermal Higgsino benchmark is excluded because its preferred mass splitting (~ 0.38 MeV) lies below the required δ ≳ 0.51–0.56 MeV. This claim is **contested** in the board (finding f‑015).  
* The Higgsino exclusion flag (True/False) derived from the driver is likewise **contested** (finding f‑015).  
* The extracted capture‑rate values are **supported**, but the associated exclusion status for the Higgsino benchmark remains unverified without driver output.

### Missing Observables
The following quantities required by the task remain unavailable:

* Effective number of neutrino species ΔN_eff for each benchmark.  
* Higgsino exclusion flag (True/False).  
* Likelihood or significance of the LZ event under each model.  
* Dark‑matter mass $m_\chi$ for the benchmarks.  

## Discussion
The extracted capture rates ($C_{\odot}=1.53\times10^{20}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ for pseudo‑Dirac and $3.98\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ for neutron‑philic) are in exact agreement with the published values, confirming that the PDF text was correctly read. However, without execution of the ASTRA driver, we cannot verify whether the code reproduces these numbers, nor can we assess the ΔN_eff predictions or the Higgsino exclusion flag. The contested status of the Higgsino exclusion highlights the need for an independent calculation (e.g., via the driver or a separate cosmology code such as CLASS) to resolve the discrepancy. The inability to extract Table 1 prevents a full quantitative comparison, limiting the validation to a qualitative check of a subset of observables.

## Limitations
* **Tool budget exhausted** before any driver execution; no generic command‑execution capability is present.  
* **No table‑extraction tool** available, so ΔN_eff and exclusion flags from Table 1 could not be obtained.  
* **HPC dispatch configuration missing**, preventing remote job submission to run the driver.  
* **No CLASS (or CAMB) installation**, precluding cross‑validation of ΔN_eff.  
* All conclusions about the Higgsino benchmark are based solely on the paper text and remain contested.

## Open directions
- **d-04** – Run the ASTRA driver with explicit logging to obtain all required observables and enable direct comparison with Table 1.  
- **d-05** – Perform a higher‑resolution scan of the capture rate $C_{\odot}$ over the mass‑splitting $\delta$ and DM mass $m_\chi$ grid to map decision thresholds.  
- **d-06** – Install and configure CLASS (or CAMB) to compute ΔN_eff for each benchmark, allowing an independent cross‑check of the driver’s ΔN_eff output.  
- **d-07** – Provide the missing driver log file and parse it to extract $\Delta N_{\rm eff}$, exclusion flags, $C_{\odot}$, $\Gamma_A$, $\delta$, $m_\chi$, and likelihood values.

brief.summary: Recent work by Di Mauro & Shaikh (2026) analyzes the LZ 248 keV nuclear-recoil event in the context of endothermic dark matter, focusing on solar-capture constraints that exclude a thermal Higgsino interpretation but allow pseudo-Dirac and neutron-philic scenarios. The analysis uses the ASTRA framework to encode model parameters, decision logic, and output observables such as the effective number of neutrino species (Delta_Neff), Higgsino exclusion status, and capture rates. The lz-dark-sector-bridge codebase implements this ASTRA spec, providing a driver script that computes these quantities and materializes results in a Lightcone directory. The literature establishes the key physical quantities (splitting delta, capture rate C_⊙, annihilation rate Γ_A, and ΔN_eff) that must be reproduced for validation.

success_criteria: A CSV file containing ΔN_eff, C⊙, Γ_A, and exclusion flags for all benchmarks is produced.
Manual spot‑check confirms that extracted values match the PDF within typographical tolerance.

suggested_directions.goal: Cross‑validate ΔN_eff using CLASS (or CAMB).
suggested_directions.rationale: Independent cosmology calculations provide a robust check on the ΔN_eff values generated by the ASTRA driver.
steps: Install CLASS (or CAMB) in the execution environment.
For each benchmark, supply the relevant particle‑physics parameters (mass, splitting, degrees of freedom).
Run CLASS to compute ΔN_eff.
Compare the CLASS output to the driver‑generated ΔN_eff; require agreement within 0.01 ΔN_eff units.
success_criteria: ΔN_eff values from CLASS are obtained for all benchmarks.
Differences between CLASS and driver values are ≤0.01.

suggested_directions.goal: Perform a limited δ–mχ sensitivity scan with the driver.
suggested_directions.rationale: A coarse scan (e.g., 3×3 grid) demonstrates how capture and annihilation rates vary with the key model parameters and informs robustness of the exclusion claim.
steps: Define a small grid of δ values (e.g., 0.4, 0.5, 0.6 MeV) and mχ values (e.g., 100, 150, 200 GeV).
For each grid point, run the driver (once step 1 is available) and record C⊙, Γ_A, and exclusion flag.
Aggregate results into a CSV and generate a heat‑map plot of C⊙ versus (δ, mχ).
Identify regions where the Higgsino benchmark becomes excluded or allowed.
success_criteria: A CSV file with observables for all nine grid points is produced.
A heat‑map plot visualising the dependence of C⊙ on δ and mχ is generated.

suggested_directions.goal: Assess the impact of alternative halo velocity distributions on C⊙.
suggested_directions.rationale: Solar capture rates are sensitive to the assumed dark‑matter velocity distribution; testing alternatives quantifies systematic uncertainty.
steps: Implement at least one alternative halo model (e.g., a Debris Flow component) in the driver input configuration.
Run the driver for the pseudo‑Dirac and neutron‑philic benchmarks under both the standard SHM and the alternative model.
Record the change in C⊙ and compute the percentage shift.
Summarise findings in a short report and, if significant, update the exclusion assessment.
success_criteria: C⊙ values for both halo models are obtained for each benchmark.
A quantitative statement of the relative change (e.g., ±X %) is produced.

suggested_directions.goal: Obtain and apply the user's ALCF HPC configuration to enable remote dispatch.
suggested_directions.rationale: Remote execution is the primary path identified for running the ASTRA driver; without valid credentials and queue information the workflow cannot proceed.
steps: Ask the user to provide ALCF username, project ID, work directory, and queue name.
Create a dispatch configuration file (e.g., ~/.dispatch.yaml) with the supplied values.
Validate the configuration by invoking a lightweight test job (e.g., `hostname` or `echo test`).
success_criteria: Dispatch configuration file is created without errors.
Test job runs successfully on the ALCF system and returns expected output.

suggested_directions.goal: Run the ASTRA driver locally with explicit logging to generate driver.log.
suggested_directions.rationale: If remote HPC is unavailable or delayed, a local run provides the required observables and a log for downstream analysis.
steps: Set up a Python virtual environment with the project's dependencies (e.g., `pip install -r requirements.txt`).
Execute `python analysis/paper9_solar_capture_analysis.py --log driver.log`.
Verify that driver.log contains entries for ΔN_eff, Higgsino exclusion flag, C_⊙, Γ_A, δ, m_χ, and likelihood.
success_criteria: driver.log file is created in the run directory.
All seven quantitative observables are present and parsable.

suggested_directions.goal: Extract Table 1 from the Di Mauro & Shaikh (2026) PDF using a dedicated table‑extraction library.
suggested_directions.rationale: Accurate numeric values from Table 1 are needed for a quantitative comparison with driver outputs.
steps: Install `tabula-py` or `camelot-py` in the analysis environment.
Run the extractor on pages containing Table 1 and output CSV/JSON.
Manually verify that the extracted rows match the PDF visual table.
success_criteria: A machine‑readable file containing ΔN_eff, C_⊙, Γ_A, and exclusion flags for each benchmark is produced.
Cross‑check with the PDF confirms no transcription errors.

suggested_directions.goal: Install and run CLASS (or CAMB) to compute ΔN_eff for each benchmark model.
suggested_directions.rationale: Independent cosmology calculation is required to cross‑validate the driver’s ΔN_eff values.
steps: Clone the CLASS repository and compile it according to the documentation.
Create parameter files for the pseudo‑Dirac, neutron‑philic, and thermal Higgsino benchmarks.
Run CLASS for each file and record the resulting ΔN_eff.
Compare the CLASS results to the driver’s ΔN_eff values (tolerance ≤ 0.01).
success_criteria: CLASS runs complete without errors for all three benchmarks.
ΔN_eff values are extracted and stored in a structured format.
Differences between CLASS and driver ΔN_eff are ≤ 0.01.

suggested_directions.goal: Perform a quantitative comparison between driver‑generated observables and the extracted Table 1 values.
suggested_directions.rationale: The core validation task is to demonstrate that the ASTRA driver reproduces the published numbers within specified tolerances.
steps: Load driver.log and the Table 1 CSV produced in the previous direction.
Compute absolute and relative differences for each observable (ΔN_eff, C_⊙, Γ_A, exclusion flag).
Flag any observable where the relative difference exceeds 5 % (or where flags disagree).
Summarize results in a report table.
success_criteria: A comparison table is generated showing all observables and their differences.
All differences are within the predefined tolerances, or deviations are clearly documented.
